introduction-buying-the-car.core: Acquiring a company means acquiring its code, infrastructure, shortcuts and vulnerabilities. Technical due diligence inspects them before the deal closes, so the price and plan reflect reality.

first_principles.problem: Buyers pay for a product and customers, then discover the platform can't scale, depends on one engineer, or has years of unpatched security holes.
truths: Fixing problems after closing is costlier.
derivation: Inspect **people, architecture, code, security, operations** before closing.
Feed findings into **price, terms and integration plan**.

analogy.title: A pre-purchase car inspection
analogy.story: You'd pay a mechanic before buying a used car; the shiny paint might hide a rusted frame.
analogy.breaks: Cars are inspected in an hour. Systems need weeks and access to people and code.

example.title: Acquiring a SaaS startup

steps.label: Value
steps.detail: Findings turned into a $3M price adjustment and a 90-day plan.

example.outcome: the buyer pays a fair price and knows the fix-up plan.

check.q: Why do TDD before closing rather than after?
check.a: Findings can still change the price, terms or decision; after closing you just own the problems.

the-due-diligence-process-data-room.core: TDD runs in a 30–90 day window after a non-binding letter of intent. The target shares documents in a data room and grants controlled access to code and people, under confidentiality.

first_principles.problem: Without a structured process, diligence teams waste weeks requesting documents, miss key areas or alarm the target's staff.
derivation: Start with a **request list** (architecture docs, incident history, security reports, costs).
Get **read-only code access** and **interviews** with key engineers.

analogy.title: A house survey before purchase
analogy.story: Within the agreed window, the surveyor gets the keys, checks documents and inspects rooms before contracts are signed.
analogy.breaks: Houses don't change during the survey. Software teams keep shipping, so findings are a snapshot.

example.title: First week of diligence

steps.label: Tip
steps.detail: Interviews with on-call engineers reveal fragile areas fastest.

example.outcome: the limited window is used efficiently.

check.q: What is an LOI in M&A?
check.a: A non-binding letter of intent stating the buyer plans to acquire at a rough price, subject to due diligence.

the-tech-stack-audit.core: Assess five pillars: people and knowledge distribution (bus factor), architecture and scalability, code quality and tests, security and compliance, and operations and cost.

first_principles.problem: Diligence teams jump into code style and miss the bigger risks: one person holds critical knowledge, or the architecture can't handle 10× growth.
truths: Knowledge concentrated in one person is a risk.

analogy.title: A building survey's checklist
analogy.story: Structure, wiring, plumbing, fire safety and running costs are all checked, not just the paint.
analogy.breaks: Buildings have codes to compare against. Software standards vary, so judge against the buyer's plans.

example.title: Bus factor of one

steps.label: Mitigation
steps.detail: Retention bonus plus documented knowledge transfer.

example.outcome: a key-person risk becomes a deal term.

check.a: The number of people who could leave before a project becomes unmaintainable.

finding-tech-debt-bombs.core: Tech debt bombs are severe hidden liabilities that will explode under specific triggers: end-of-life dependencies, unscalable designs, missing backups, licence violations or key-person dependencies.

first_principles.problem: Everyday tech debt is expected. Bombs are different: invisible now but catastrophic when growth, a departure or an EOL date arrives after you've paid.
truths: Triggers are often predictable (EOL dates, growth).

analogy.title: A ticking timer in the basement
analogy.story: Everything upstairs seems fine; downstairs a timer counts down to a known date.
analogy.breaks: Bomb timers are visible once found. Tech bombs need targeted searching.

example.title: EOL database version
example.scenario: Target runs a database version out of support next quarter.

steps.label: Report
steps.detail: Clear trigger date, cost and impact for leadership.

example.outcome: the bomb is priced and scheduled for defusing.

check.q: Give two examples of tech debt bombs.
check.a: An end-of-life database version and untested backups.

integration-risks-culture-clash.core: Most acquisition value is lost during integration, often through the 'rewrite trap' (forcing the acquired product onto the buyer's stack) and culture clashes that drive key engineers away.

first_principles.problem: The buyer insists the acquired Python/GCP product be rewritten on its Java/AWS platform. Two years later the product has stagnated and its best engineers have left.
truths: Value lies in the product working, not its stack.
derivation: **Avoid forced rewrites**: integrate at boundaries (APIs, SSO, data).
**Retain key people** with clear roles and autonomy.

analogy.title: Merging two kitchens
analogy.story: Forcing the acquired restaurant's chefs to cook your menu with your equipment loses what made their food good, and the chefs.
analogy.breaks: Recipes can be written down. Product knowledge lives in people, which is why retention matters so much.

example.title: Integrating a GCP startup into an AWS company

steps.label: Retention
steps.detail: Founding engineers keep ownership of their product.

check.a: Forcing an acquired product to be rebuilt on the buyer's stack, which destroys value and drives away engineers.

the-tdd-findings-report.core: The findings report translates technical risks into business impact for executives and lawyers: severity, likelihood, cost to fix, timeline and recommended deal action (price, terms, walk away).

first_principles.problem: A report full of jargon ('no HPA, single-AZ RDS') doesn't help a CFO decide whether to spend $50M.
truths: Money and time are shared language.
derivation: For each: **business impact, cost and time to fix, deal recommendation**.

analogy.title: A home survey summary
analogy.story: "Roof needs replacing within 2 years: £15k. Recommend reducing the offer." No roofing jargon needed.
analogy.breaks: Survey costs are fairly standard. Software remediation estimates carry more uncertainty, so give ranges.

example.title: A critical finding
example.scenario: No tested backups for the customer database.

steps.label: Plain language
steps.detail: "Customer data could be permanently lost; fix before closing."

example.outcome: executives can act on technical risk.

check.q: What should every finding include for executives?
check.a: Business impact, cost and time to fix, and a recommended deal action.
